Śāṇḍilya Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
Though considered a minor Upaniṣad and assigned to the Atharvaveda group, the Śāṇḍilya Upaniṣad is a fairly large work dealing exhaustively with a complicated subject, viz., योग.
There are three adhyāyas or chapters. Each chapter is divided into khaṇḍas (small sections) containing mantras, both in prose and in verses. There are 14 khaṇḍas and 147 mantras in all.
The first adhyāya containing 11 khaṇḍas and 120 mantras is not only the biggest but also occupies almost the whole book.
The second—the smallest—has only one khaṇḍa and 6 mantras.
The third has 2 khaṇḍas and 21 mantras.
First Chapter
Khaṇḍa 1 (14 mantras)
The Upaniṣad begins with a question on aṣṭāṅgayoga (yoga with eight limbs or steps) by शाण्डिल्य to his teacher, the sage Atharvaṇa. He replies that the eight steps are: यम (restraint), नियम (observances), आसन (posture), प्राणायाम (control of vital currents), प्रत्याहार (state of withdrawal), धारणा (concentration), ध्यान (meditation) and समाधि (total absorption).
Yama is of ten kinds. They are: अहिṁसा (non-injury), सत्य (truth), अस्तेय (non-stealing), ब्रह्मचर्य (continence), दया (compassion), ārjava (straight forwardness), kṣamā (forgiveness), dhṛti (steadiness), mitāhāra (moderation in eating) and शौच (cleanliness). Each of these is clearly defined.
Khaṇḍa 2 (11 mantras)
This describes ten kinds of niyamas. They are: तपस् (austerity), सन्तोष (contentment), āstikya (faith in the वेदस्), दान (giving gifts), īśvarapūjana (worship of God), siddhāntaśravaṇa (listening to the Vedāntic scriptures), hrī (modesty), mati (faith in Vedic rituals), जप (repetition of the मन्त्र given by the गुरु) and vrata (following the injunctions of the वेदस्).
Khaṇḍa 3 (15 mantras)
Eight kinds of āsanas are delineated here in detail.
These āsanas are: स्वस्तिक, गोमुख, पद्म, vīra, siṁha, bhadra, mukta and mayūra.
By practising them properly one can get rid of all the diseases of the body.
Khaṇḍa 4 (14 mantras)
This is a highly technical and complicated section giving a lot of information about the following aspects of yogic sādhanas or practices: number and positions of the various nāḍīs in the human body; on the suṣumnānāḍī; the कुण्डलिनी and its nature as also its movement; the ten prāṇas (vital airs) and their functions.
Khaṇḍa 5 (4 mantras)
The qualifications of a person who wants to practise योग are set forth in the first मन्त्र. Self-control, detachment. devotion to truth, obedience to the parents and the गुरु are stressed greatly.
There is also a nice description of a place fit for establishing a मठ (hermitage) suitable to the practice of योग. Natural beauty, and availability of water, fruits, roots and flowers are the deciding factors. The next part deals with the preliminaries connected with प्राणायाम.
Khaṇḍa 6 (5 mantras)
This small section is devoted to प्राणायाम. The practical method of connecting the three stages of प्राणायाम viz., रेचक, पूरक and कुम्भक, with the three syllables of praṇava—akāra, ukāra and makāra—as also the meditation on the three aspects of देवी (Gāyatrī, सावित्री and सरस्वती) are described here.
Khaṇḍa 7 (52 mantras)
This is a long section dealing almost exclusively with various disciplines mentioned in the works on हठयोग. They may be very briefly summarised as follows.
Cleansing of the सुषुम्ना nāḍī; number and methods of प्राणायाम; rules regarding ड़ोओद् during sādhana; caution; how to attain steadiness of मिन्द् through कुम्भक; various bandhas and mudras (See BANDHA and MUDRĀ.); dissolution of मिन्द् and कैवल्य through योग including प्राणायाम; सिद्धिस् (supernatural powers) as also attaining good health through various saṁyamas (See SAṀYAMA for details).
Khaṇḍa 8 (2 mantras) and Khaṇḍa 9 (1 मन्त्र)
Five kinds of pratyāhāras and five varieties of dhāraṇās are described here.
The pratyāhāras are: withdrawing the मिन्द् from the इन्द्रियस् (senses); the results of prescribed actions; all objects, and, marmasthānas (sensitive places) in the body.
The dhāraṇas (methods of fixing the मिन्द्) are: fixing the मिन्द् on the inner Self; imposing the external sky on the internal sky (daharākāśa, the space in the region of the heart) and superimposing the five aspects of ब्रह्मन् (Pañca-brahma; See PAÑCABRAHMAMANTRAS.) on the five elements like earth, water etc.
Khaṇḍas 10 and 11 (1 मन्त्र each)
Two kinds of ध्यान (meditation)—saguṇa (on God with form) and nirguṇa (on the आत्मन्)—are described in the tenth khaṇḍa.
The eleventh deals with समाधि or total absorption wherein the unity and identity of the जीव (individual सोउल्) with परमात्मन् (God) are experienced giving infinite bliss.
Second Chapter
This has only one khaṇḍa with six mantras.
It contains the usual description of ब्रह्मन् as found in the उपनिषद्स् and treatises on Advaita Vedānta such as:
It is without attributes. Hence it cannot be defined. It is beyond the comprehension of speech and मिन्द्. Whatever exists, is that Pramātman. It can be realised through the instructions from a proper गुरु or spiritual teacher.
Third Chapter
Khaṇḍa 1 (6 mantras)
This section opens with a question by शाण्डिल्य to Atharvaṇa as to how ब्रह्मन्, the one without a second, can become this universe of multiplicity.
In reply, the sage Atharvaṇa declares that ब्रह्मन् has three rūpas or forms: niṣkala (without parts), sakala (with parts) and sakala-niṣkala (with and without parts).
In its own essential nature ब्रह्मन् is चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् and bliss, actionless, pure, all-pervading, extremely subtle and beyond all चोग्नितिओन् and immortal. This is its niṣkala form.
But by using its natural, inscrutable power of māyā which has the three guṇas inherent in it, it becomes महेश्वर (the great ruler). This is its sakala form.
However, when महेश्वर wills to create and become many, through jñānamaya-तपस् (austerity of knowledge or intense thinking), he becomes this universe of names and forms such as the वेदस् and Vedic fires, the gods, the living beings, the varṇas and so on. He being in the form of all gods, living beings, existing in their hearts as also beyond, is ‘sakala-niṣkala’.
Khaṇḍa 2 (15 mantras)
The highest Truth is called ब्रह्मन् since it is the greatest (= bṛhat). It is also the आत्मन् (in everyone) since it pervades everything (= āpnoti) or includes everything in itself (atti = eats up). It is this ब्रह्मन्/Ātman that is known as दत्तात्रेय since it was born as the son of the sage अत्रि and his wife अनसूया.
Then there is a beautiful description of God as दत्तात्रेय. One who meditates on him as ‘I am He’ becomes a knower of ब्रह्मन्. He becomes liberated from all sins.

Śaṇḍa
------------------------------------------
Śaṇḍa and Amarka were the sons of शुक्राचार्य, the गुरु of the राक्षसस् (demons). When he went away for तपस्, शण्ड and Amarka acted as the priests of the demon-king हिरण्यकशिपु. They were also the teachers of प्रह्लाद, हिरण्यकशिपु’s son and a great devotee of विष्णु (Vide Bhāgavata 7.5; Viṣṇupurāṇa 1.17).

Śāṇḍilyavidyā
(‘science taught by शाण्डिल्य’)
------------------------------------------
In the Chāṇdogya Upaniṣad (3.14) ब्रह्मन् is described as tajjalān. A description of this ब्रह्मन्, both as the transcendent and the immanent reality followed by the fruit of meditating on him are given here. This knowledge is known as Śāṇḍilyavidyā since it was first taught by the sage शाण्डिल्य.
See VIDYĀS for details.

Ṣaṇmukha
(‘the six-faced one’)
------------------------------------------
See SUBRAHMAṆYA.

Śāṇḍilya
------------------------------------------
The problem with the ancient Hindu scriptures is that we come across the same name—especially that of a ṛṣi or sage—in a number of places, obviously belonging to different periods of time. The name शाण्डिल्य (son or descendant of Śaṇḍila) is one such.
Several Śāṇḍilyas that we find in these scriptures may be listed as follows:
Śāṇḍilya is mentioned several times in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (9.4.4.17; 10.1.4.10) as a great authority of अग्नि-cayana (fire-ritual) where his अग्नि (fire) has been called Śāṇḍila’. He was the teacher of Vātsya and a pupil of Kuśrī.
According to other lists of lineage, several sages have been mentioned as his teachers. Some of them are: Kaiśorya कश्यप, Vaiṣṭapureya, गौतम and so on.
In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (3.14) an important teaching of शाण्डिल्य is given. It has been called Śaṇḍilyavidyā.
One शाण्डिल्य is mentioned in the Mahābhārata several times as a sage in the court of युधिष्ठिर (Sabhāparva 4.17). His opinion on दान (giving gifts) has been quoted in the Anuśāsanaparva (65.19).
The author of an ancient treatise on भक्ति or devotion (the Bhaktisūtras of शाण्डिल्य) was also a शाण्डिल्य. The work is actually known by his name as Śāṇḍilyaśatasūtrīyam. Two more works— Śāṇḍilyopaniṣad and Śāṇḍilyasaṁhitā—are also attributed to him.

Śāṇḍilya भक्ति Sūtras
------------------------------------------
The Doctrine of भक्ति was not imported
In his preface to his इन्दिअन् फिलोसोफ्य्, Vol. I, Dr. S. Radhakrishnan writes: ‘Ignorance of the subject of Indian thought is profound. To the modern मिन्द् इन्दिअन् फिलोसोफ्य् means two or three “silly” notions about māyā, or the delusiveness of the world, kama, or belief in fate, and त्याग, or the ascetic desire to be rid of the ﬂesh. Even these simple notions, it is said, are wrapped up in barbarous nomenclature and chaotic clouds of vapour and verbiage, looked upon by the “natives” as wonders of intellect. After a six months’ tour from Calcutta to चपे चोमोरिन्, our modem aesthete dismisses the whole of Indian culture and philosophy as “pantheism,” “worthless scholasticism,” “a mere play upon words,” “at all events nothing similar to Plato or Aristotle, or even Plotinus or Bacon.”
No wonder that such Western scholars have traced the origin of the doctrine of भक्ति (or devotion to God) to Christian ideas and inﬂuences. Even E. B. Cowell who has done yeomen service to the cause of इन्दिअन् फिलोसोफ्य् by his pioneering works through his translations of Sarvadarāanasaṅgraha, न्यायकुसुमाञ्जलि and Śāṇḍilyaśatasūtrīya is constrained to write in his preface to the last—mentioned work thus: ‘Dr. Lorinser, Prof. Lassen, and Prof. Weber have maintained that the doctrine of भक्ति arose in India as a more or less direct reﬂection of Christian ideas. I cannot pretend to speak positively on the controversy; I would only confess to a some-what hesitating inclination towards Prof. Weber’s moderate opinion on the question.’ Of course, these views have been contradicted by other scholars who have made a more dispassionate study of Indian thought. Garbe says in his Philosophy of Ancient India. ‘For one who is intimate with the intellectual life of ancient India the doctrine of भक्ति is entirely conceivable as a genuine product of India. No shadow of evidence has up to now been brought forward to support the theory that the conception of भक्ति is derived from Christianity. The religious significance contained in the word भक्ति has nothing exclusively about it that is specially Christian. Not only have devotion to God and faith in Him developed themselves gradually in other monotheistic religions, but even beyond the circle of monotheistic ideas, the two conceptions are to be found. And, particularly in India, we possess all the essentials on the strength of which we have to regard भक्ति as “indigenous” fact, as Barth says, since monotheistic ideas are to be found prevalent from the time of the ऋग्वेद onward through almost all the periods of the religious history of India, and the powerful longings for the Divine, peculiar to the Indian सोउल् from yore, must have developed such sentiments as divine love and divine faith in a popularly conceived monotheism.’ इन्दिअन् फिलोसोफ्य् by Dr. S. Radhakrishnan, Vol. I, pp. 499-502.">1
Its Vedic Origin
Actually the doctrine of भक्ति is as old as the ऋग्वेद itself. While commenting on the aphorism ‘bhakti prameyā śrutibhyah’ स्वप्नेश्वर’s version of the original.">2 (Śāṇḍilya भक्ति Sūtras

) Sri Nārāyana Tīrtha has accumulated quite a mass of unassailable evidence to prove its Vedic origin. Take for instance this ṛk where the Lord has been praised and there is also a reference to the recitation of his names: ‘You praise that Ancient Cause, the Origin of rta (the Divine Law), according to your knowledge. You will be freed from birth. If you cannot praise him, recite his name. However, we, O Lord Vienu, devote ourselves to your light and attributeless form!’ (Ṛgveda 1.156.3) And again, this ṛk where there is a clear allusion to the hearing and reciting of His names as also surrender to Him: ‘He who offers (his all) to Lord Visnu, the husband of Śrī (or लक्ष्मी), the Ancient Cause, the Creator, the Ever-new, he who recites the glorious birth and works of this glorious Being, that giver, that reciter, obtains fame (or material enjoyments) and reaches the Highest Abode.’ (ibid. 1.156.2) Another ṛk considers इन्द्र the great God as ड़थेर् and मोथेर्: ‘O Vasu! 0 Śatakratu! You have become our ड़थेर्! You are मोथेर्! So now we bow down to you!’ (ibid. 8.98.11)
Coming to the Upanisads we see that though they are mainly devoted to knowledge, the doctrine of grace which is an important aspect of the philosophy of devotion, is evident as for instance, in this statement of the Ka_tha Upanisad: ‘Whom the Âtman chooses, by him, is He obtained; to him He reveals Himself ’ (2.23). So also in another: ‘When he who is devoid of desire-motivated actions, through the grace of God the supporter, sees the परमात्मन्’s glory, then does he become freed from sorrow’ (ibid. 2.20). The Śvetāśvatara Upanisad actually uses the word भक्ति and clearly states प्रपत्ति (self-surrender) also: ‘He who has supreme devotion (bhakti) towards God, and as towards God so towards the teacher, to him verily, the great सोउल्, all these things declared (thus far) will reveal themselves’ (6.23); ‘To Him who at the beginning created ब्रह्मा, and who gave the वेदस् to him, to Him the God who reveals the knowledge of Himself, desirous of लिबेरतिओन्, do I ﬂy for refuge’ (6.18).
The भागवत Religion
Gradually the doctrine of भक्ति was systematised into a regular philosophy and religion. It came to be known as the Bhāgavata—religion and has also been variously designated as the Nārāyar_fiya, सात्वत, Ekāntika, or Pāñcarātra religion. सात्वत means a devotee of Krsna. Ekānfika means single—minded devotion.">3 Its main sources are the Nārāyanīya section of the महाभारत, the Vienu Purāna, the भगवद्गीता, the भागवत Purāna, the Pāñcarātra Âgamas and the भक्ति Sūtras of शाण्डिल्य and नारद.
Not being satisfied with the impersonal ब्रह्मन् of the Upanisads, the भागवत religion has converted ब्रह्मन् into the Personal God. ईश्वर, Nārāyana and Krsna-वासुदेव are the names most commonly used with respect to him. He cannot be apprehended by the senses nor by लोगिच् and arguments. Srutis or the scriptures at best point towards him. His grace is the supreme factor in realising him. Singleminded devotion (ekāntikabhakti) is the only thing by which his grace can be obtained and he can be captured. Actually he is not independent as others make him out to be, because, he is subject to the will of his devotees (bhaktaparādhÏna). He is always fond of those devoted to him and reveals himself to them. Complete resignation (prapatti or śaranāgati) is another means of attain— ing him. These are its chief tenets in brief.
The Sūtras of नारद and Śāṇdilya
In Sanskrit literature it is commonly seen that the propounder of any doctrine or philosophy, or for that matter, any branch of knowledge, puts it down in the form of sūtras or aphoristic statements which are supposed to be brief but pregnant with deep meaning. Either his disciples or those coming in that tradition generally compose more detailed explanations of those sūtras called variously as bhāsya, vrtti, vārttika or ṭikā, depending upon their length or form. It is impossible to understand these sūtras properly without the help of such traditional commentaries. Since this sūtra literature along with the respective commentaries forms the basic work in any branch of knowledge it is usual for the students of that branch to make a deep study of them. Looking from this standpoint, it is imperative that serious students of the doctrine of devotion must make a careful study of both the नारद भक्ति Sūtras and the शाण्डिल्य भक्ति सूत्रस्. Before we delve deeper into the latter which is the subject of this essay, it is worthwhile making a brief comparative study of these two.
Though both the works are associated with the names of two great sages who adorned the spiritual horizon of our country, though there are no doctrinal differences between them, and though they deal with the subject in a more or less systematic way, their mode of approach to the subject is so different that we are compelled to say that each is complementary to the other and that our study of devotion will not be complete without studying both of them. शाण्डिल्य’s approach is more intellectual while नारद’s is more emotional and practical. Hence we can safely say that शाण्डिल्य has evolved a philosophy of devotion whereas नारद has made it a practical religion of devotion. शाण्डिल्य is very particular in mentioning the pramānas (the means of knowledge) as also the nature and mutual relationship among the various constituents of the prameya (what is to be known) like Īśvarā, जीव and prakrti. He discusses about the reality of च्रेअतिओन्, controverts the theory that knowledge alone can give लिबेरतिओन्, propounds and defends devotion as the sole means of लिबेरतिओन् and also delineates the various forms of devotion. नारद however does not seem to be interested a whit in all these intellectual gymnastics but goes straight to the practical aspects. Apart from defining devotion and describing its various forms, he gives several invaluable practical hints, warns against the pitfalls, eulogises the importance of devotion, gives its special characteristics to enable the aspirants to imitate them and finally paints a vivid picture of the ideal devotees.
When we look at the sūtras of जैमिनि, पतञ्जलि or Bādarāyana, we would perhaps be more right in putting the sūtras of शाण्डिल्य in that class. May be for the same reason, several commentators have chosen to comment upon these sūtras and leave नारद’s untouched. Neither do the latter need any commentary since they are so simple and direct.
It would however be extremely interesting, and even fascinating, if an attempt could be made to intelligently synthesise the two into a single treatise on devotion.
Śāṇḍilya, the Sūtrakāra
The ancient Indian मिन्द् seems to be sweetly indifi‘erent to ‘history.’ If an oriental scholar of the West is prepared to devote his whole life-time to collect exact historical data regarding a Śar‘1kara’s date of birth, just to know whether he was born in A.
or A.

the Indian pundit would begin to trace ‘his story’ to the promised descent of Lord शिव (who is also known as Sankara) in कैलास! That is why Dr. S. Radhakrishnan says 4 that the problem of determining the exact dates of early Indian systems is ‘as fascinating as it is insoluble and it has furnished a field for the wildest hypotheses, wonderful reconstruction and bold romance.’ The problem of our शाण्डिल्य is no exception to this.
If we can just manage to forget the well-known Vedic dictum, êatāyurvai puru5ah (‘Man lives but hundred years’), we will be amazed to find our शाण्डिल्य almost in every age! In the त्रेतायुग we find him as the spiritual guide of king दिलीप. In the द्वापरयुग, he is the priest to the king नन्द of the cowherds. In the beginning of this कलियुग, he is very busy performing the Putresti sacrifice of Śatānīka, the son of जनमेजय. At one time he is the priest of king त्रिशङ्कु. At another time he is seen. chatting with Bhīsma, the grand old man of the महाभारत sitting on his bed of arrows! He is also the ड़थेर् of Safikha and लिखित, the two well—known authors of a smrti.
Neither can we fall back on the Upanisads which contain his name, since there are three 8āndilyas mentioned in the B_rhadāranyaka 5 alone, and since the dates of these Upanisads themselves have not been determined with any accuracy so far. There is a well-known passage in the छान्दोग्य उपनिषद् 6 which goes by the name शाण्डिल्यविद्या which is also referred to in the Śār_zdilya भक्ति Sūtras. But the commentator says that it refers to an earlier शाण्डिल्य. Nor is there any definite internal evidence in the sūtrawork itself.
However, there is some evidence available, though very fragile, with the help of which we may just limit the period of his existence. शाण्डिल्य has been quoted as an author in the Pāñcarātra literature. The author of these भक्ति Sūtras also belongs to the Pāñcarātra school since that is the philosophy propounded here. He » draws upon the Bhagavad गीता freer and even directly mentions it once. 7 Therefore he comes definitely after the age of the महाभारत.
Although the भागवत Purāna occupies almost a central place in this भागवत cult there is no direct reference to it anywhere in the sūtras. Even Svapnesīvara, the earliest commentator on these sūtras, has not quoted from it except once (sū. 72) and that too not having any direct bearing on the sūtra itself, though he quotes profusely from the Visnu Purāna. It is only Nārāyana Tīrtha that finds a reference to the भागवत in the sū. 84 while interpreting the words tathā hyāha. Since स्वप्नेश्वर supplies a more apt quotation from the गीता to this very sūtra, we need not take Nārāyana Tīrtha’s reference very seriously. Hence we would not be wrong if we say that शाण्डिल्य existed before the composition of the भागवत which is normally assigned to A.
. This limits his existence to the period between 500 B. C. and A.

.
Two sages, कश्यप and Bādarāyana, are mentioned in the sūtras 29 and 30. Bādarāyana is mentioned again in sū. 91. It is well—known that he is the author of the Vedānta Sūtras, though nothing definite can be said about कश्यप. Indian scholars put the lower limit of the date of these sūtras to 200 B. C.
Then, there is definite and clear reference to the योग system of पतञ्जलि in the sū. 19. The words ‘samādhi’ (sū. 20) and ‘klista’ (sū. 33) belong to yogic terminology. Hence the योग of पतञ्जलि must have been a well—known system by the time of शाण्डिल्य. According to scholars the योग Sūtras must have been composed anywhere between 200 B. C. and A.

. Since there are clear indications 8 that our author believed in the सत्कार्यवाद (the doctrine of the pre-existance of the effect in the cause), and also a few other doctrines of the Sāṅkhya school, and since the earliest work of this system viz., Sāṅkhya Kārikā of Īśvarakrsna is assigned to the 3rd century A. D., शाण्डिल्य’s date is now restricted to the period between A.

and 900.
There are two other works, शाण्डिल्य Sarñhitā and Śāndilyopaniead, associated with the name of शाण्डिल्य. But nothing can be said definitely whether our sūtrakāra was their author.
Svapneśvara, the Bhāgyākara
The earliest extant commentary on the sūtras of शाण्डिल्य is that by स्वप्नेश्वर. It has been traditionally known as the Bhāsya. In fact, स्वप्नेश्वर himself has christened it so. 9
In trying to determine his date, we meet with almost similar difficulties since there is scant evidence on which to base our conclusions. He has quoted the भागवत only once in his commentary (sū. 72) by which we can guess that he comes after the age of the भागवत. But, since he has not quoted profusely, though there was plenty of scope for that, we are constrained to say that this purāna had not as yet attained the fame and status as it did in later years. Nārāyana Tīrtha, a later commentator refers to a commentary on the sūtras by Śrī
Rāmānuja. 10
Granting that this is the famous acārya of Viêistādvaita and since स्वप्नेश्वर does not seem to be aware of this commentary, we may say that स्वप्नेश्वर existed between A.

and 1000.
But then, there is another difficulty. It is definitely known that स्वप्नेश्वर wrote a work called Kaumudīprabhā इन्दिअन् फिलोसोफ्य् Vol. II, p. 255, footnotes 3.">11 wherein he refers to the Sāṅkhya Prava— cana Sūtra and assigns it to पञ्चशिख instead of कपिल as the tradition goes. 12 Scholars are almost unanimous in assigning this latter work to the 14th century A. D. Again, Nārāyana 'I‘īrtha (17th century A. D.) often refers to the views of स्वप्नेश्वर especially when he is difi‘ering from him. Hence we will have to conclude that स्वप्नेश्वर must have existed between the 14th and the 17th centuries, much nearer the 14th than the 17th.
Svapneśvara belongs to Bengal. He himself says in the closing verse to his commentary that he is the son of J aleśvara who was the commander-in—chief of kings and that Jaleśvara was the son of Viśārada, the sovereign monarch of the Gaudadeśa (i.e., Bengal). While quoting from the Abhijñāna Śākuntala (see sū. 6) he has given the Gauda recension. This also confirms that he was a native of Bengal.
His opening and closing verses show that he was a great devotee of Śrī Krsna.
His commentary on the sūtras is simple and gives a natural explanation. It occupies the same place in antiquity and importance with respect to the शाण्डिल्य भक्ति सूत्रस् as the Bhā5ya of व्यास on the योग Sūtras of पतञ्जलि.
He himself mentions two of his works wherein he says, he has discussed the subject of the pramānas in greater detail. 13 They are: Nyāyatattvanikasa and Vedāntatattvanikaṣa. Unfortunately neither of the works is available now.
Other Commentators
Two other commentaries have so far been discovered and published: The Bhakticandrikā of Nārāyana 'I‘īrtha and another one by Bhavadeva. '
Nārāyana Tīrtha Was an advaitic monk and lived in the latter half of the seventeenth century at Vārānasī. He was a disciple of श्रीराम Govinda Tīrtha and had his एदुचतिओन् under one वासुदेव. He was a very great scholar and has ten other works to his credit which include two commentaries on मधुसूदन सरस्वती’s Siddhāntabindhu, two on the Sāṅkhyan treatises, Tattvakaumudī and साङ्ख्यकारिका, one commentary each on the योग Sūtras and Nyāyakusumāñjdli of उदयन and another work on devotion, Bhaktyadhikaranamālā.
His Bhakticandrikā is very exhaustive and replete with quotations, especially from the भागवत. His interpretations are elaborate and often independent of Svapneāvara’s views though at times he elucidates his Bhāgya also. It is evident that he has drawn largely upon Madhusūdana’s Bhagavad-भक्ति-rasāyana.
It is interesting to note that Nārāyana Tīrtha while commenting on the sūtras 32 and 33, refers to the interpretation of Sri रामानुजाचार्य. 14 Since Srī Rāmānuja’s life and works are well preserved in the annals of his Mathas and since nothing has been heard of his having ever written a commentary on the शाण्डिल्य Sūtras this statement of Nārāyana Tīrtha is intriguing. It is perhaps worthwhile making some research in this direction.
Another factor to be noted in Bhakticandrikā is that it gives three additional sūtras which are not in स्वप्नेश्वर’s version, but omits one from the latter. 15
Other Bhaktisūtras
Śrī बलदेव उपाध्याय in his Sanskrit introduction to the excellent edition of Bhakticandrikā refers to two other sūtra-works on भक्ति which he has appended at the end: Bhaktimīmāmsā and Parabhaktisūtrāni. The former is a work of the thirteenth century and consists of 102 sūtras, divided into four chapters, each chapter being subdivided again into two pādas. Śrī उपाध्याय thinks that this work belongs to the भागवत cult and follows very closely the doctrines of the Muktāphala of बोपदेव. The latter is the work of Svāmī Hariharāranya, a well— known scholar on योग. It is a short work of only 26 sūtras and is divided into four āhnikas.
The Philosophy of Sār_quilya भक्ति Sūtras
Let us now turn to the philosophy of शाण्डिल्य as depicted in his sūtras, depending mainly on the Bhā.ṣya of स्वप्नेश्वर. For the sake of convenience in understanding the philosophy of the sūtras, the same can be discussed under four main headings: a) The Pramānas or means of knowledge; b) The Prameyas or the objects to be known through these means; c) The sādhanas or the practical means to be adopted to gain लिबेरतिओन् and d) मुक्ति or absolute लिबेरतिओन् from mundane existence.
A) THE PRAMÀNAS
Though the philosophy of the sūtras स्वप्नेश्वर appear to be bhedābhedavādins, accepting both difference and nondifi‘ereuœ between the individual souls and God, difference in the state of bondage and non difference in the state of लिबेरतिओन्.">16 seems to have a close affinity with the Advaita Vedānta of Sankara, only three means of knowledge like the three eyes of रुद्र are accepted, as against the six of the Sankara school. They are pratyaksa or sense-perception, अनुमान or inference, and sabda or verbal testimony of the scriptures, the last one being the chief. In sense-perception an important point to be noted is that knowledge through it comes in two stages: When the senses come into contact with their objects, the इग्नोरन्चे covering them is first destroyed, and then only, knowledge will arise in the मिन्द् due to its being illumined by the सोउल्.
B) THE PRAMEYAS
Īśvara or God, जीव or the individual सोउल् and jagat or the created world are the three prameyas we come across in the work as in other theistic treatises.
Īśvara, पर, cit and bhajanīya are the words used in the sūtras to denote God. Devotion to him gives लिबेरतिओन् and not knowledge of him. His sakti or power is called māyā or prakrti. He creates the world through this māyāśakti, putting it up as a screen as it were. Hence it is this prakrti that undergoes modifications and not he himself. Since he and his power are identical, this च्रेअतिओन् also is identical with him. His power is unobstructed. He is ever the Lord and ever free. He is of the nature of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्. He, out of pity for the created beings, takes on a divine body through his power and is born in the world out of his own free will in order to destroy the demons or propagate the वेदस्. In fact after creating the world consisting of the high and the low, he also, like a ड़थेर्, creates the वेदस्.
There are several well-known incarnations of his, devotion to whom also give libera— tion. Though there are several modes of devotion even one is enough to please him if practised intensely. When devotees give up their bodies in this world before attaining supreme devotion to him, they are reborn in his world where they will continue their practice and ultimater attain him. He is the dispenser of the fruits of our actions, of our merit and demerit.
The individual सोउल् or जीव is of the nature of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् and is essentially identical with God, also called ब्रह्मन् by the commentator. His individuality, his separation from God, has been caused by his association with बुद्धि or antahkarana (intellect or internal organ) which consists of the three gunas and is an उपाधि (a limiting adjunct). Again this association and the consequent bondage of sarhsāra have been caused by lack of devotion to God - and ‘ not by lack of knowledge of him. Being an evolute of the prakrti of God, which is real, this उपाधि is also real and not an इल्लुसिओन् caused by इग्नोरन्चे. Hence it cannot be removed by knowledge. When a red china rose is kept near a crystal and the crystal appears red, it cannot be got rid of however intently or cleverly one may gaze at it! 17 It can be removed only by the removal of either of the two things or the contact between them. Similarly' here also. Since the सोउल् is eternal and all-pervading, the only other alternative left is to dissolve this उपाधि viz., the बुद्धि back into its original cause, the prakrti of God. This can be done only by supreme devotion to God. Once this is done, लिबेरतिओन् is attained. Though the individual सोउल् is actually identical with God, because of the multiplicity of the buddhis, it also appears as many. It is like the sun appearing as many, being reﬂected in several mirrors. When the mirrors are removed, the several reﬂections are merged back in the sun. It is for this very reason, that when one सोउल् is liberated, others are not, like the reﬂections continuing in other mirrors even though one is removed.
Apart from the conscious entity which exists in a two—fold form (God and individual सोउल्), the only other reality that exists is the insentient prakrti. There is no third reality apart from these two.
This prakrti is actually the power (śakti) of God and is also called māyā and प्रधान. It functions also as the material cause for च्रेअतिओन्. Being the power of God, it is real and not unreal as some others think. Hence this world, the whole च्रेअतिओन्, which is its product or effect, is also real. Arguing back-wards, prakrti is the generality or totality of insentient च्रेअतिओन्. Hence it pervades everyone of its products. But being insentient, it cannot by itself evolve into this wonderful universe. Neither can the intellect of an ordinary being do it. It is possible only for God. The order in which च्रेअतिओन् takes place from God is practically the same as in the Sāf1khya and the Vedānta systems. Dissolution takes place in the reverse order.
The sūtras uphold the ‘sat—kārya-वाद’ or the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect in the cause and the consequent pervasion of the former by the latter. Hence च्रेअतिओन् (srsti) and destruction (pralaya) are actually manifestation (āvirbhāva) and disappearance (tirobhāva). The doctrine of production (utpatti) which says that the effect is a new product, produced by the combination of the causes, is criticised and disapproved.
C) THE SÀDHANÂS
Bhakti or devotion is the sole means to लिबेरतिओन्. It is defined as supreme attachment to and love for
God. 18

All, down to despised souls, are entitled to tread the path of devotion.
This devotion is not of the nature of knowledge (jñāna) for these reasons: i) It is lacking in the knowledge of one who hates. One who hates another may have knowledge about him, but he cannot be said to be devoted to him! ii) Knowledge gradually gets eclipsed as devotion arises; iii) It is the opposite of hatred. Hatred being an emotion, devotion also must be likewise. It is well-known that the opposite of hatred is love and not knowledge; iv) Devotion is spoken of as a रस which is the same as राग or attachment, and as anurāga which clearly means attachment to God; v) Lastly, there is the famous example of the milkmaids of Vrndāvana who attained लिबेरतिओन् through devotion even though they had no knowledge.
Though devotion is of the nature of राग (attachment), it cannot for that reason be condemned, because the object of that attachment is God and not human beings or the things of the world. It is only in the latter case that it becomes condemnable.
Neither can it be identified with work (kriyā), will or wish (icchā), nor even with faith (śraddhā).
Then, what is the place of knowledge in the scheme of लिबेरतिओन्? It is a secondary sādhanā which helps to destroy the impurities of मिन्द् and thus pave the way for the rise of devotion.
It is interesting to note that शाण्डिल्य calls the प्रस्थानत्रय (the Upanisads, the गीता and the वेदान्तसूत्रस्) as Brahmakār_zda and not as Jñānakār_zda as it is usually termed. He argues that ज्ञान or knowledge is common to both the Pūrvamīmārñsā (called Karmakānda) and the Uttaramīmāmsā. In both cases the object is to give us the knowledge about things which are previously unknown: of कर्म (ceremonial rites) in the former case and of ब्रह्मन् in the latter case. After giving this knowledge the former urges us to perform these rites and the latter, to attain लिबेरतिओन् through devotion to ब्रह्मन्, termed as sarhsthā. शाण्डिल्य, devotion. See sū.3.">19
The path of योग as taught by पतञ्जलि is also useful as a secondary discipline since it helps in the purification and concentration of मिन्द्. However the समाधि (perfect concentration) spoken of there, can also be attained by secondary devotional practices. Precisely for these reasons a devotee of God is superior to those who tread the path of concentration, ceremonial rites or knowledge.
Śāṇḍilya has graded devotion into two varieties: parā or supreme and gaur_fi or secondary. Actually it is the former alone that deserves to be named as भक्ति. Since the latter leads to the rise of the former, it is also called भक्ति, but in a secondary (gaunī) sense.
In sū. 44 शाण्डिल्य gives a long list of the signs by which the maturity of devotion can be inferred. They are: sammāna (respect), bahumāna (high esteem), prīti (delight), viraha (forlornness), itaravicikitsā (doubting other objects), mahimakhyāti (praising His greatness), tadartha— prānasthāna (holding the life for His sake), tadīyatā (considering everything as His), sarvatadbhāva (regarding Him as existing in all beings) and aprātikūlya (not resist— ing His will).
Though these are the signs by which supreme devotion expresses itself, they are also the means to attain supreme devotion when they are consciously prac— tised 20. In the latter case they become guaṇibhakti.
Other types of secondary devotion are those mentioned in the गीता (9th chapter) such as कीर्तन (praising God) नमस्कार (obeisance), ananyacintana (thinking of none else but him), yajana 21 (worshipping him), patrādidāna (offering of leaves, ﬂowers etc.), arpana (offering everything one does or enjoys) etc.
All these purify the heart and facili— tate the rise of supreme devotion. There is no rule that they should be practised all together or only some of them or in any particular order. Anyone when practised sincerely and intensely can please God and thus gives rise to supreme devotion.
Most of these forms of secondary devotion are of the nature of action; for instance, worshipping him with all the accessories, singing his glories, repeating his names and so on. Among all forms of action these are the best, since they are actually the result of the meritorious acts of previous births and will now lead directly to supreme devotion. Another beauty of these is that they can produce either supreme devotion or fulfil any other desire of the aspirant depending upon his attitude and motive.
The scriptures contain elaborate and difficult expiations for various kinds of sins. They consume a lot of time and ‘ money as also cause a lot of physical pain. The doctrine of भक्ति assures that remembrance of God, glorifying him, hearing about his life and deeds etc., are also equally capable of destroying even great sins and can be a substitute for those difficult expiations.
However a sincere repentence is a precondition and these practices must be continued till death. And for a sinner, the real practice of devotion will begin only after the destruction of his sins through remembrance etc.
Supreme devotion (parābhakti or parānurakti) which rises in the final stages as a result of the practice of secondary devotion leads to infinite beatitude. A very important characteristic of this devotion is ekāntabhāva or absolute one—pointedness This devotion can be directed not only towards God but also towards any of his manifestation like Varāha, Nrsifi1ha, वामन, राम or शिव.
Since all, irrespective of their birth or capacity, are entitled to the practice of devotion, it is likely that many of them will not have attained supreme devotion before they die. Such devotees are reborn in the world of God like the श्वेतद्वीप where they will continue their devotional practices and finally attain it, and through it, लिबेरतिओन्.
D) M UKTI
It is the lack of this supreme devotion that is the real cause of bondage, of sufÏ‘ering and transmigration, and not lack of knowledge as some argue. The commentator does not subscribe to the Advaitic view of anirvacanīyakhyāti (logical inde— finability of a particalar type of knowledge) with the help of which the illusoriness of the world is sought to be proved. When a snake is seen in a rope it is a simple case of mistake technically called अन्यथाख्याति (mistaking one for another). Hence it is lack of devotion alone, and not knowledge, that is the cause of bondage. Consequently devotion destroys this bondage and gives लिबेरतिओन्. That this libera— tion is of the nature of इम्मोर्तलित्य् and is obtained through devotion to God is confirmed by the śrutis also (vide Chāndogya Upanigad 223.2).
Supreme devotion destroys the उपाधि of the individual सोउल् viz., the बुद्धि (understanding) or antahkarana (the internal organ) thereby liberating it. The liberated सोउल् lives as a jīvanmukta as long as the body lasts due to the momentum of his past karmas which have fructified giving him this body. Once the body falls, he is merged in God.
It has already been pointed out that this is like the merging of the reﬂected image of the sun in the real sun once the mirror is removed, and other non-liberated souls will continue to exist separately due to the upādhis being infinite in number.
Liberation can also take place in a gradual way. Those who are purified by the practice of lower forms of devotion but die before getting supreme devotion, will go by the arcirārdimārga (the path of light leading to the world of conditioned ब्रह्मन्) and reach final beatitude from there, later on. Thus, lower devotion gives gradual लिबेरतिओन् whereas supreme devotion gives it immediately. However, it should not be forgotten that even lower devotion leads to लिबेरतिओन् only through the production of supreme devotion whether in this world or in the higher region.
Conclusion
For seekers of लिबेरतिओन् through the path of devotion, a study of the शाण्डिल्य भक्ति सूत्रस् is of great help since it can generate intellectual conviction about the efficacy of भक्ति as a system of sādhanā.
In addition, if नारद भक्ति Sūtras is also studied, it can supplement many useful modes of sādhanās to the ones given by the former work.
